runs.question: How does the NIST Generative AI Profile describe data privacy risks?

answer.text:
NIST AI 600-1 covers this in section 2.4, "Data Privacy." (Search was unavailable, so I read the pages directly.) It opens by saying GAI systems raise several risks to privacy. It describes these risks:

- **Training data and privacy principles:** GAI training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. Using personal data this way raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose specification.
- **Lack of disclosure:** Most model developers do not disclose the specific data sources their models were trained on. This limits user awareness of whether PII was trained on and, if so, how it was collected.
- **Leakage and memorization:** Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals. During adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information from the public domain that was in their training data. This is called data memorization, and it may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present in only a small number of training samples.
- **Inference of new information:** GAI models may correctly infer PII or sensitive data that was not in their training data and was not disclosed by the user, by stitching together information from disparate sources. These inferences can harm an individual even when they are inaccurate (e.g., confabulations). The harm is greater if they reveal information the person considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.
- **Downstream harms:** Beyond harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm), wrong or inappropriate inferences of PII can contribute to downstream or secondary harms. For example, predictive inferences based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups.

The profile also links privacy to other risks. For example, training data memorization in GAI outputs could infringe copyright if the training data included copyrighted material. It also notes that GAI-generated obscene, abusive or degrading content can create privacy, psychological and emotional, and even physical harms.

citations.cited_text: GAI system training requires large volumes of data, which in some cases may include personal data. The use of personal data for GAI training raises risks to widely accepted privacy principles, including to transparency, individual participation (including consent), and purpose speciﬁcation.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, most model developers do not disclose speciﬁc data sources on which models were trained, limiting user awareness of whether personally identiﬁably information (PII) was trained on and, if so, how it was collected. Models may leak, generate, or correctly infer sensitive information about individuals.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, during adversarial attacks, LLMs have revealed sensitive information (from the public domain) that was included in their training data. This problem has been referred to as data memorization, and may pose exacerbated privacy risks even for data present only in a small number of training samples.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: In addition to revealing sensitive information in GAI training data, GAI models may be able to correctly infer P II or sensitive data that was not in their training data nor disclosed by the user by stitching together information from disparate sources.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: These inferences can have negative impact on an individual even if the inferences are not accurate (e.g., confabulations), and especially if they reveal information that the individual considers sensitive or that is used to disadvantage or harm them.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: Beyond harms from information exposure (such as extortion or dignitary harm), wrong or inappropriate inferences of PII can contribute to downstream or secondary harmful impacts.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 11
citations.cited_text: For example, predictive inferences made by GAI models based on PII or protected attributes can contribute to adverse decisions, leading to representational or allocative harms to individuals or groups (see Harmful Bias and Homogenization below).

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 15
citations.cited_text: Intellectual Property Intellectual property risks from GAI systems may arise where the use of copyrighted works is not a fair use under the fair use doctrine. If a GAI system’s training data included copyrighted material, GAI outputs displaying instances of training data memorization (see Data Privacy above) could infringe on copyright.

citations.title: NIST AI 600-1: AI Risk Management Framework, Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024, page 15
citations.cited_text: GAI-generated obscene, abusive or degrading content can create privacy, psychological and emotional, and even physical harms, and in some cases may be illegal. Generated explicit or obscene AI content may include highly realistic “deepfakes” of real individuals, including children.
